title: How the Internet Works for Designers

questions.prompt: Which best describes what IP guarantees?

options.text: Reliable, ordered delivery of every packet
Addressing and routing on a best-effort basis, with no delivery guarantee
Encryption of all traffic
That packets arrive exactly once

questions.explanation: IP handles addressing and routing but is best-effort. Reliability and ordering are added by TCP on top of IP.

questions.prompt: When is UDP a better choice than TCP?

options.text: When every byte must arrive in order (e.g., a file download)
When timeliness matters more than guaranteed delivery (e.g., live video)
When you need automatic retransmission of lost data
When you need a reliable connection handshake

questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless and low-overhead. For live media, delivering on time beats delivering everything, so a lost packet is skipped rather than resent.

questions.prompt: What does TLS add on top of HTTP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confidentiality (encryption)
Integrity (tamper detection)
Authentication of the server via a certificate
Faster routing of packets

questions.explanation: TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. It does not change how packets are routed.

questions.prompt: DNS answers are stored for a period defined by their ______, so most lookups are served from cache. (acronym or word)
questions.explanation: The TTL (time-to-live) controls how long a DNS answer is cached before it must be looked up again.

questions.prompt: A service makes 10 sequential calls to a database across an ocean, each a ~100 ms round trip. Why is this slow regardless of database speed?

options.text: Databases are inherently slow
Latency is dominated by the number of round trips, so 10 x ~100 ms = ~1 second of pure network time
TCP encrypts each call
UDP would lose the packets

questions.explanation: Ten sequential round trips add up to ~1 second no matter how fast the database is. Batch the calls or co-locate the components.

questions.prompt: How does a CDN reduce latency for a global audience?

options.text: It compresses the database
It caches content on edge servers near users, so requests reach a nearby edge instead of a distant origin
It replaces TCP with UDP
It removes the need for DNS

questions.explanation: A CDN serves cached content from an edge location close to the user, turning a ~150 ms trip to the origin into a few milliseconds.
